fetched_contents.text: Evaluation of cowpea cultivars for intercropping with pearl millet in the Sahelian zone of West Africa Skip to main contentSkip to article * Access through your organization * Purchase PDF Abstract Field trials were conducted at ICRISAT Sahelian Centre, Niger, to examine the performance of contrasting cowpea cultivars intercropped with pearl millet. Significant effects (P ≤ 0.05) of cropping system and cultivars were observed for cowpea grain yield. Cultivar × cropping system interaction was significant only for fodder yield. Intercropping reduced cowpea yields significantly but the degree of reduction varied among cultivars. Early-maturing erect cultivars exhibited greater yield reduction than the indeterminate spreading types and had the least effect on millet yields. Indeterminate spreading cultivars produced greater grain and fodder yield than erect types and caused the greatest millet yield reduction. The relationship between the yield of cowpea cultivars and millet when intercropped was negative. Linear correlations between yield of cowpea in sole and intercrop were positive and significant (P < 0.01) with r values ranging from 0.45 to 0.91. However, a small proportion of the greatest and least-yielding cowpea cultivars in intercropping would have been selected and rejected, respectively, on the basis of sole-crop grain-yield. It was concluded that selection of cowpea cultivars for intercropping with millet based on their grain yield in sole crop may have limited success. Selection based on fodder yield favoured late-maturing cultivars. Selection of cowpea cultivars for intercropping should be based on their intercropped performance, paying special attention to other agronomic factors. An appropriate cowpea cultivar for intercropping with millet would be the one that is less competitive with millet and yields both grain and fodder. fetched_contents.text: Intercropping millet with low-density cowpea improves millet productivity for low and medium N input in semi-arid central Senegal Abstract Cereal-legume intercropping has been traditionally practiced across West Africa by farmers and provides resilience of agriculture to climate variability. Intensification of these extensive intercropping systems in order to meet future food demand is critical. This study aims at evaluating the agronomic performance of the intensification of millet-cowpea intercropping with low cowpea density, and its variation with climate variability, using an on-station experiment in Bambey, Senegal. Two trials (irrigated vs rainfed) were set up to compare millet sole- and inter-cropping with a grain and a fodder variety of cowpea, in 2018 and 2019. Two levels of fertilization were tested: 0 kg(N) ha−1 and 69 kg(N) ha−1. The two cropping years were contrasting and water stress around flowering and/or during grain filling (indicated by the Fraction of Transpirable Soil Water) was higher in 2019 than in 2018 in the rainfed experiment. In both experiment and for all treatments, land equivalent ratio (LER) in the intercropping was 1.6 and 1.4 for grain and biomass respectively. Millet aboveground biomass was significantly higher in intercropping than in sole cropping in the irrigated experiment but not in the rainfed experiment. In the rainfed experiment, the interaction between cropping system and year was significant, so that millet aboveground biomass was greater in intercropping than in sole cropping in 2018 (year of lower water stress) but not in 2019 (year of higher water stress). The effect of fertilization on millet aboveground biomass did not significantly interact with cropping system (sole vs intercrop). For grain yield, fertilization interacted significantly with the cropping system in the irrigated trial: the benefits of intercropping on millet grain yield were greater with 69 kg(N) ha−1 than with 0 kg(N) ha−1. This significant interaction could not be observed in the rainfed trial, potentially due to water stress. These results show that the level of water stress (related here to the year and to the rainfed or irrigated experiment) and that of fertilization modulate the performance of millet-cowpea intercropping in the semi-arid context of Senegal. Overall, fertilization had a stronger effect on millet grain yield than intercropping. The two strategies (intercropping and mineral fertilization) can be complementary to achieve sustainable intensification of cropping system in semi-arid areas of West Africa. Introduction Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) faces food insecurity with cereal crop yield lower than in other regions of the world [1,2], mostly because of nutrient limitations [3]. Increase in droughts and the corresponding more frequent water and heat stresses is expected to further constrain crop production [4,5]. Arable land being limited, ecological intensification is a promising pathway to improve food security and farm income while minimizing negative impact of agriculture on the environment by harnessing the biological processes regulating primary production [[6], [7], [8]]. Diversification of cropping systems helps maintaining regulatory services and coping with risks resulting from the inter-annual variability of climate [e.g. Ref. [9]]. Diversification of cropping systems can be achieved with intercropping. In the tropical world, particularly in SSA, intercropping is a widespread practice [10]. Intercropping favors complementarity and facilitation between intercropped species for the use of environmental resources and contributes to improve systems productivity [11]. Intercropping a cereal with a legume is the most common strategy, as it can provide grain for human consumption and fodder for livestock [12,13]. Under semi-arid climate, farmers and researchers see it as a promising option to cope with climate variability [14]. However, the benefits of intercropping originating from facilitation between the component species may not always be fully realized, depending on the climate of a specific year. For example, in their modelling study [15] suggested that sorghum and cowpea competed for water in drier years, while nitrogen stress prevailed in the wetter years. More experimental work is thus needed to unravel the impact of climate variability and water stress on intercropping performance. The interplay between the fertilization of the cereal and the performance of the cereal-legume intercropping is also a controversial topic: while some studies show that the benefit of intercropping decreases with fertilizer N inputs [11], others show that these benefits are maintained, even at greater fertilizer N inputs [16]. More experimental work on the impact of the intensification of cereal-legume intercropping is therefore required to unravel the impact of soil, climate, and crop management. Pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum (L.) R. Br.) is one of the main cereal crops in Senegal: 80,744 tons were produced in 2019 reprensenting 29% of national cereal production [17]. The millet variety Souna is generally grown by farmers under rainfed conditions with little or no inputs, resulting in low yields of about 0.5–0.6 t/ha, well below the potential yield of circa 3 t/ha with that same variety. This potential could be further increased if varieties with higher potential harvest index were made available to farmers [18]. Population growth in Senegal is 3% per year, which means a doubling of population in two decades. Given the limited scope for expanding the area under cultivation, this will pose huge challenges to food security in the near future. The “old groundnut basin” is the country's grain basket. The interplay between the fertilization of the cereal and the performance of the cereal-legume intercropping is also a controversial topic: while some studies show that the benefit of intercropping decreases with fertilizer N inputs [11], others show that these benefits are maintained, even at greater fertilizer N inputs [16]. More experimental work on the impact of the intensification of cereal-legume intercropping is therefore required to unravel the impact of soil, climate, and crop management. Pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum (L.) R. Br.) is one of the main cereal crops in Senegal: 80,744 tons were produced in 2019 reprensenting 29% of national cereal production [17]. The millet variety Souna is generally grown by farmers under rainfed conditions with little or no inputs, resulting in low yields of about 0.5–0.6 t/ha, well below the potential yield of circa 3 t/ha with that same variety. This potential could be further increased if varieties with higher potential harvest index were made available to farmers [18]. Population growth in Senegal is 3% per year, which means a doubling of population in two decades. Given the limited scope for expanding the area under cultivation, this will pose huge challenges to food security in the near future. The “old groundnut basin” is the country's grain basket. In the most arid northern half of this region, the typical cropping system is a biennal millet –groundnut rotation with millet as the staple crop, frequently intercropped with cowpea (Vigna unguiculate), sown at very low density. Cowpea is chosen by farmer because it is a good quality fodder for livestock, and it also provides a protein-rich staple for human consumption [19]. This study aims at exploring the scope for intensified millet-cowpea intercropping. We evaluate the agronomic performance of millet-cowpea intercropping with and without N fertilizer inputs and with and without water stress. In doing so, we explore the hypotheses that i) intercropped millet produces more grain and biomass than sole millet, and ii) the benefits of intercropping is maintained with water stress and at greater N fertilizer input, and hence it is a crucial component of sustainable intensification of cropping systems in the region. 2. Experimental site The study was conducted in Senegal at the experimental station of the National Center for Agronomic Research of Bambey (14°42′48″ N, 16°28′ 47″W) during two growing seasons, in 2018 and 2019. The climate in this area is predominantly Sahelo-Sudanian with annual rainfall ranging from 400 to 900 mm. During these two years of experimentation, the rainy season began at the end of June. The cumulative rainfall was 448 mm in 2018 and 488 mm in 2019. Average temperatures ranged from 21 °C to 42.5 °C (Fig. S1). The soil in the experimental plot is tropical ferruginous with sandy-silt texture. Average total N content in the topsoil was 0.03%, and average C was 0.34%. Cowpea variety traits that matter most for yield in millet-cowpea intercropping are best summarized as trait combinations that reduce competition with millet while maintaining productivity. The evidence points most directly to early maturing cultivars and low-density cowpea types as favorable in intercropping, because they are associated with less millet yield reduction and/or better system performance.

Early-maturing cowpea cultivars are repeatedly linked to better intercropping outcomes. The Sahelian millet-cowpea study found that “early-maturing erect cultivars exhibited greater yield reduction” than indeterminate spreading types, but also noted that “indeterminate spreading cultivars produced greater grain and fodder yield than erect types and caused the greatest millet yield reduction” [N1-F1]. This is important because it shows that maturation timing and plant architecture matter: erect types may have higher biomass or yield in sole cropping, but are more competitive with millet. In contrast, late-maturing cultivars are favored for fodder yield, according to the same source, and are therefore better suited when the goal is to balance millet yield with cowpea productivity [N1-F1]. A separate study on cowpea variety effects on millet grain and above-ground biomass also supports that cowpea variety choice alters outcomes, with intercropping reducing cowpea yields but the degree of reduction varying among cultivars [N1-F1]. The cited “Evaluation of cowpea cultivars for intercropping with pearl millet in the Sahelian zone of West Africa” is therefore a central source for this trait conclusion [N1-F1].

Biomass is another trait that appears relevant, though the evidence is more indirect. The Sahelian study notes that intercropping reduced cowpea yields significantly, but the degree of reduction varied among cultivars [N1-F1]. It also states that “selection of cowpea cultivars for intercropping with millet should be based on their intercropped performance, paying special attention to other agronomic factors” [N1-F1]. This suggests that biomass, or at least the overall agronomic profile, is important. A later Senegalese intercropping study found that millet aboveground biomass was higher in intercropping than in sole cropping in the irrigated experiment, but not in the rainfed experiment [N1-F2]. It also found that the interaction between cropping system and year was significant, indicating that biomass outcomes depend on both crop type and environmental conditions [N1-F2]. However, biomass in cowpea itself is not directly quantified in the provided excerpts, so the strongest evidence for biomass as a yield trait is indirect.

Pod number and seed size are not directly supported in the provided evidence. The excerpts emphasize yield reduction, competition effects, and variety-specific responses, but they do not isolate pod number or seed size as a major determinant of intercropping yield [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Therefore, the evidence base is thin on these traits.

Variety choice affects resource use and competition with millet mainly through competition intensity. The Sahelian study reports that intercropping reduced cowpea yields significantly and that the degree of reduction varied among cultivars [N1-F1]. It further states that “indeterminate spreading cultivars produced greater grain and fodder yield than erect types and caused the greatest millet yield reduction,” implying that erect or early-maturing types are less competitive with millet [N1-F1]. A separate study on millet-cowpea intercropping with low-density cowpea found that millet aboveground biomass was higher in intercropping than in sole cropping in the irrigated experiment, while the rainfed experiment showed less consistent improvement [N1-F2]. This suggests that cowpea density and spacing influence resource use and competition, but the excerpt does not distinguish cowpea pod number or seed size from these effects [N1-F2]. The general mechanism is therefore one of resource competition and tradeoff between cowpea and millet, with variety choice altering how strongly those tradeoffs manifest [N1-F1].

In terms of variety types most commonly recommended in field studies, the evidence points to low-density cowpea varieties and indeterminate spreading types. The Senegalese study compares millet sole cropping with intercropping using a grain and a fodder variety of cowpea [N1-F2]. It also emphasizes that low-density cowpea improves millet productivity for low and medium N input in semi-arid central Senegal [N1-F2]. A separate study explicitly states that “an appropriate cowpea cultivar for intercropping with pearl millet would be one that was weakly competitive and that yielded both grain and fodder” [N5-R3]. This is especially relevant because it indicates that breeders and farmers should prioritize cowpea cultivars that are not highly competitive but still productive in intercropping systems [N5-R3]. Early-maturing erect cultivars are not recommended as the best overall intercrop type, because they caused the greatest millet yield reduction in one source [N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear hierarchy of traits: early-maturing or low-density cowpea types are generally more favorable in millet-cowpea intercropping because they reduce millet yield loss and may improve system performance [N1-F1][N5-R3]. Indeterminate spreading types can yield more cowpea in intercropping but are more competitive with millet [N1-F1]. Biomass is relevant, but not directly quantified in the provided excerpts [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Pod number and seed size are not strongly supported in the evidence set [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The most commonly recommended variety types in the field studies are therefore low-density cowpea and cultivars that are weakly competitive and produce both grain and fodder [N1-F2][N5-R3].

Cowpea growth duration influences intercropping yield outcomes primarily through its effect on resource competition and harvest timing. The evidence indicates that longer or shorter duration can either intensify competition or reduce it, depending on how the cowpea’s growth period aligns with millet’s growth stages and how much canopy cover is established over time.

Shorter duration tends to reduce millet yield loss because cowpea is present for less time and therefore competes less intensely. The Sahelian study states that millet yields were reduced less when sown simultaneously with early cowpea cultivars than when sown with a late-maturing local cultivar [N1-R3]. A later Senegalese study similarly reports that millet aboveground biomass was higher in intercropping than in sole cropping in the irrigated experiment, while the rainfed experiment showed less consistent improvement [N1-F2]. This suggests that cowpea duration interacts with millet growth stages: if cowpea finishes growing before millet reaches peak competition, millet may suffer less yield reduction. The same source also notes that the interaction between cropping system and year was significant, indicating that duration effects depend on environmental conditions [N1-F2].

Longer duration can intensify competition, particularly when cowpea shading or biomass accumulation occurs before millet can fully occupy its space. The evidence on planting timing and cowpea intercrop growth indicates that delaying sowing of cowpea relative to millet can reduce crop growth rates and yield because cowpea faces shading and increased competition from already established millet [N2-R2]. Another study on millet/cowpea intercropping in semi-arid Mali reports that delayed sowing of the legume reduced interspecies competition [N6-R4]. This supports the idea that longer cowpea duration can worsen competition if cowpea establishes too late and then competes more strongly with millet as it grows. The Senegalese study also notes that intercropping may reduce cowpea yields significantly, with the degree of reduction varying among cultivars [N1-F1], which implies that longer or more vigorous cowpea growth can suppress millet more than shorter-duration types.

Light, water, and nutrient competition are all affected by duration. The Sahelian study states that “intercropping reduced cowpea yields significantly but the degree of reduction varied among cultivars” and that “indeterminate spreading cultivars produced greater grain and fodder yield than erect types and caused the greatest millet yield reduction” [N1-F1]. The Senegalese study adds that cowpea grain yield was strongly linked to water supply, and that intercropping can reduce cowpea yield while the degree of reduction varies among cultivars [N1-F2]. This indicates that water competition is a key constraint in intercropping, especially when cowpea duration is longer and shading or biomass accumulation is greater. The evidence also suggests that nutrient competition is important, because intercropping is described as altering resource use and yield outcomes [N1-F1][N1-F2]. However, the provided excerpts do not isolate nutrient competition as a separate mechanism in the same detail as light and water.

Duration can determine harvest timing and millet yield tradeoffs. The Senegalese study reports that millet aboveground biomass was higher in intercropping than in sole cropping in the irrigated experiment, but not in the rainfed experiment [N1-F2]. It also notes that the effect of fertilization on millet aboveground biomass did not significantly interact with cropping system in the irrigated trial, while the interaction was significant in the rainfed trial [N1-F2]. This shows that duration and planting timing can shape when millet reaches its maximum biomass and whether the intercropping system improves output. The timing of cowpea establishment relative to millet also matters: delayed sowing reduced cowpea growth rates and yield [N2-R2]. This means that harvest timing is not fixed by millet alone; cowpea duration can shift the balance between millet and cowpea maturity, changing the tradeoff between the two crops.

The evidence for duration thresholds that improve or reduce total output is mixed but suggestive. In the Sahelian study, early-maturing cowpea reduced millet yield loss compared to late-maturing cultivars [N1-R3]. In the Senegalese study, low-density cowpea improved millet productivity in semi-arid central Senegal [N1-F2]. These results suggest that shorter-duration cowpea can improve millet yield, especially when cowpea density is low. However, the rainfed experiment showed less consistent improvement, indicating that duration thresholds depend on water availability and year-to-year variability [N1-F2]. The evidence also shows that some cowpea cultivars can reduce millet yield more than others, so there is no single threshold that universally improves output; instead, the optimal duration depends on the system and environmental context [N1-F1][N1-F2].

In summary, cowpea growth duration influences intercropping outcomes mainly through resource competition and harvest timing. Shorter duration tends to reduce millet yield loss, while longer duration can intensify competition, especially when cowpea shading or biomass accumulation occurs before millet can fully occupy its space [N1-R3][N2-R2][N6-R4]. Light, water, and nutrient competition are all affected, with water competition appearing especially prominent in the evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Duration can determine harvest timing and millet yield tradeoffs, but the evidence does not provide a precise universal threshold; instead, it points to context-dependent improvements when cowpea duration and density are aligned with millet growth stages and environmental conditions [N1-F2][N2-R2][N6-R4].

The practical implications of cowpea variety choice are that variety effects are amplified under certain environmental and management conditions, especially when cowpea density, planting timing, and crop sequence interact with millet’s growth pattern. The evidence indicates that variety choice matters most strongly when the system is semi-arid, low-input, or when water stress and fertilizer availability vary by year [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Environmental conditions that amplify variety effects include semi-arid climate, low and medium nitrogen input, and water stress. The Senegalese study states that millet-cowpea intercropping improves productivity for low and medium N input in semi-arid central Senegal and that the benefits of intercropping depend on water stress [N1-F2]. It also notes that the interaction between cropping system and year was significant, so the same variety can perform differently under contrasting climate conditions [N1-F2]. The Sahelian study similarly emphasizes that intercropping reduces cowpea yields significantly, but the degree of reduction varies among cultivars, and that cowpea yield is strongly linked to water supply [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that variety effects are amplified under drought or water-stressed conditions, where competition for water becomes more intense.

Management conditions that amplify variety effects include planting density, spacing, and crop sequence. The Senegalese study compares millet sole cropping with intercropping using a grain and a fodder variety of cowpea, and it reports that low-density cowpea improves millet productivity [N1-F2]. It also finds that millet aboveground biomass was higher in intercropping than in sole cropping in the irrigated experiment, but not in the rainfed experiment [N1-F2]. This indicates that cowpea density is a critical management variable: lower density reduces competition and can improve millet performance. A separate study on cowpea intercrop growth and yield as affected by time of planting relative to millet reports that delaying sowing reduced crop growth rates and yield because cowpea faced shading and increased competition from already established millet [N2-R2]. This shows that planting timing and crop sequence matter: sowing cowpea earlier or later relative to millet changes the competition dynamics.

Spacing and crop sequence modify the impact of variety choice by altering resource capture and competition. The Senegalese study explicitly compares two trials with low-density cowpea and finds that intercropping improves productivity under low and medium N input [N1-F2]. The same study also notes that the interaction between cropping system and year was significant, which implies that spacing and intercropping design can shift outcomes depending on environmental conditions [N1-F2]. Another study on millet/cowpea intercropping in semi-arid Mali reports that rotating millet/cowpea intercrops with sole millet increased the grain yield of sole millet by 30%, and that delayed sowing of the legume reduced interspecies competition [N6-R4]. This supports the idea that crop sequence can weaken competition and improve millet yield by changing how cowpea and millet occupy the field over time.

Recommendations for farmers and breeders based on the evidence are practical and context-specific. For farmers, the evidence suggests that low-density cowpea is generally favorable in semi-arid conditions because it improves millet productivity and reduces competition [N1-F2]. It also suggests that early sowing of cowpea can help avoid shading and reduce competition with millet [N2-R2]. For breeders, the evidence points to selecting cowpea cultivars that are weakly competitive and produce both grain and fodder [N5-R3]. The Sahelian study also recommends selecting cowpea cultivars based on intercropped performance rather than sole-crop performance, because the best sole-crop cultivars may not be the best intercroppers [N1-F1]. Additionally, the Senegalese study indicates that fertilization can modulate intercropping performance, especially under water stress [N1-F2]. This means that breeders should consider not only yield traits but also resource-use efficiency and compatibility with millet.

Overall, the practical implications are that variety choice matters most under semi-arid, low-input, or water-stressed conditions [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Management conditions such as low cowpea density, early planting relative to millet, and crop rotation can reduce competition and improve millet yield [N1-F2][N2-R2][N6-R4]. Farmers should favor low-density cowpea and early sowing, while breeders should prioritize cowpea cultivars that are weakly competitive and produce both grain and fodder [N1-F2][N5-R3]. The evidence does not support a one-size-fits-all recommendation, because outcomes depend on year-to-year variability, water stress, and fertilizer availability [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Variety-specific crop cycle effects and intercropping design constraints show that cowpea’s growth length interacts with millet’s growth stages, planting density, relay timing, and harvesting decisions. The evidence suggests that shorter crop cycles can fit better with low-density cowpea and semi-arid systems, while longer cycles may increase competition if they overlap too much with millet’s critical growth periods.

Crop cycle length interacts with millet growth stages and intercropping design primarily through timing of establishment and resource capture. The Senegalese study states that low-density cowpea improves millet productivity for low and medium N input in semi-arid central Senegal [N1-F2]. It also reports that millet aboveground biomass was higher in intercropping than in sole cropping in the irrigated experiment, but not in the rainfed experiment [N1-F2]. This implies that cowpea cycle length can affect how resources are captured over time. The study also notes that the interaction between cropping system and year was significant, meaning that the same cowpea variety can perform differently depending on when millet and cowpea occupy the field [N1-F2]. The Sahelian study similarly emphasizes that cowpea yield is strongly linked to water supply, and that the degree of reduction in cowpea yield due to intercropping varies among cultivars [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that cowpea’s growth cycle must align with millet’s growth stages to avoid excessive competition.

Early or late maturing cowpea fits better with planting density and relay timing depending on the system goal. The evidence indicates that early-maturing cowpea can reduce millet yield loss compared to late-maturing cultivars [N1-R3]. Taken together, the four branches support a clear integrated conclusion: **cowpea variety choice in millet-cowpea intercropping is a matter of balancing productivity with weak competition**. In short, the choice of cowpea variety matters most when the system is semi-arid, low-input, or when water stress and fertilizer availability vary by year.
